subject: mlops
question: Do green latency and error dashboards show the assistant is giving good answers?

artifact.description:
An LLM support assistant is monitored with: request rate, p95 latency, HTTP error rate. All dashboards are green.
AI: "Everything is green, so the assistant is working well."

ai_claim: Yes. Requests succeed quickly without errors, so the assistant is working well.

ai_solution.text: So the assistant is working well.

failure.misconception: Measuring service health but not answer quality
failure.explanation: An LLM can return fast, successful HTTP responses that are wrong, ungrounded, off-policy or unhelpful. None of the dashboards measures quality. Add quality monitoring: sampled human or LLM-judge reviews against a rubric, groundedness checks for RAG, user feedback and escalation rates, and alerts on changes.
failure.why_convincing: For traditional services, health metrics are a good proxy for 'working'.

canonical_solution: No: health metrics cannot detect wrong answers. Monitor answer quality (sampled evaluation, groundedness, feedback).

valid_evidence.summary: After a prompt change, 18% of answers cite the wrong refund policy while all dashboards stay green.
LLM applications need quality monitoring in addition to operational metrics.

counterexamples: Wrong answers are delivered quickly and successfully.

hints.text: Ask what the dashboards measure.
Step 4 equates health with quality.
Quality must be measured directly for generative systems.
Imagine a prompt change that breaks policy answers.
Step 4 is wrong: nothing measures answer quality.

repair: Add sampled quality reviews, groundedness metrics, feedback tracking and quality alerts.
debrief: For LLM apps, 'up' and 'right' are different questions. Monitor both.

subject: mlops
question: Is logging full prompts with customer details to a third-party tool the right setup?

artifact.description:
For debugging, the LLM gateway sends every full prompt and response - including customers' names, phone numbers and account details - to a third-party observability SaaS, retained for 1 year.
AI: "Full logs are essential for debugging LLM apps, so this is the right setup."

ai_claim: Yes. Complete prompts and responses are needed to debug LLM behaviour, so sending them all to the observability tool is right.

ai_solution.text: Debugging needs to see prompts and responses.
So this is the right setup.

failure.misconception: Copying personal data into a third-party log store
failure.explanation: The logs replicate customers' personal and account data to an external vendor for a year, expanding who can access it and creating privacy and compliance exposure (and breach risk). Redact or pseudonymise PII before logging, log metadata by default, restrict full-content logging to sampled, access-controlled storage with short retention, and review the vendor's data processing terms.

canonical_solution: No: raw PII flows to a third party for a year. Redact before logging, sample, restrict access and shorten retention.

valid_evidence.summary: Logs contain names, phone numbers and account details, retained 1 year by a third party.
Data minimisation: collect and retain only the personal data needed, for as short a time as needed.

counterexamples: A vendor breach exposes a year of customer conversations.

hints.text: Ask where the personal data ends up and for how long.
Step 2 values completeness over privacy.
Observability pipelines are data flows subject to privacy rules.
List who can access the vendor's logs.
Step 2 is wrong: raw PII goes to a third party. Redact and minimise.

repair: Redact PII at the gateway, sample full-content logs into restricted storage with short retention.
debrief: Every log is a copy of the data. Design LLM observability with privacy from the start.

subject: mlops
question: Does using the floating alias safely give automatic improvements?

artifact.description:
The application calls the provider's model alias 'fast-latest', which the provider updates to newer model snapshots from time to time.
The team's evaluation suite was last run three months ago.
AI: "Using the latest alias means we always get improvements automatically."

ai_claim: Yes. Newer model snapshots are better, so the alias gives the application automatic improvements with no downside.

ai_solution.text: The alias points to the newest snapshot.

failure.misconception: Depending on a model version that can change without testing
failure.explanation: A new snapshot can change output format, tone, refusal behaviour or accuracy on your specific task, even if it is better on average. With a floating alias, these changes reach production untested, and results become irreproducible. Pin a dated snapshot, and upgrade deliberately after running your evaluation suite.
failure.why_convincing: Model upgrades are usually improvements overall.

canonical_solution: No: behaviour can change unannounced for your task. Pin a snapshot and upgrade after evaluation.

valid_evidence.summary: After an alias update, the model starts wrapping JSON in Markdown fences and the parser fails for 7% of requests.
Production dependencies, including model versions, should be pinned and upgraded deliberately.

counterexamples: An unannounced snapshot change breaks output parsing.

hints.text: Ask what 'better on average' means for your task.
Step 2 assumes every update helps this application.
Pin versions; upgrade after evaluation.
Consider an output-format change.
Step 2 is wrong: updates can break your use case. Pin a snapshot.

repair: Pin a specific model snapshot and run the eval suite before switching.
debrief: Model versions are dependencies. Pin them like any other.

subject: mlops
question: Is reviewing the monthly invoice sufficient cost monitoring?

artifact.description:
An LLM feature's usage and cost are not tracked per request.
A prompt change added a 6,000-token policy document to every request; nobody noticed for three weeks.
AI: "Costs are fine: the provider invoice arrives monthly, and we can review it then."

ai_claim: Yes. The invoice shows total spend, so any cost problem will be visible when it arrives.

ai_solution.text: Cost problems appear on the invoice.

failure.explanation: A monthly invoice reveals a problem up to a month after it starts and cannot tell which feature, prompt version or customer caused it. The 6,000-token addition multiplied input tokens for three weeks unnoticed. Track tokens and cost per request, per feature and per prompt version in real time, with budgets and alerts on changes.
failure.why_convincing: The invoice does eventually show the total.

canonical_solution: No: monthly totals are too late and too coarse. Track per-request tokens and cost with alerts.

valid_evidence.summary: Average input tokens rose from 900 to 6,900 per request after the prompt change.
Cost is an operational metric; monitor it at request granularity with alerts.

counterexamples: Three weeks of inflated cost pass before anyone notices.

hints.text: Ask how quickly the invoice would reveal the change.
Step 3 relies on a monthly, aggregate signal.
Token usage should be monitored per request and per prompt version.
Compute tokens before and after the change.
Step 3 is wrong: the invoice is late and coarse. Track tokens in real time.

repair: Log tokens and cost per request with dimensions (feature, prompt version) and set alerts.
debrief: LLM costs scale with prompt design. Make token usage visible where prompts change.

subject: mlops
question: Is the AI right that this plan covers the main ways a RAG assistant can fail?

artifact.description:
RAG assistant monitoring:
- retrieval: share of queries with at least one chunk above a relevance threshold; top-k sources per answer
- answers: weekly sample of 200 graded for groundedness and correctness by trained reviewers
- users: thumbs-down rate and 'contact human' rate by topic
- documents: index freshness (hours since last successful ingestion)

ai_claim: Yes. It watches retrieval quality, answer groundedness and correctness, user dissatisfaction by topic, and stale indexes - covering retrieval failures, generation failures and data freshness.

ai_solution.text: Retrieval metrics catch queries with no relevant context.
Sampled grading measures groundedness and correctness.
User signals reveal problems by topic.

canonical_solution: Correct. RAG failures arise in retrieval, generation and data; this plan monitors each.

valid_evidence.summary: index freshness alert at 36 hours -> ingestion job failing -> answers citing outdated prices

hints.text: List the components of a RAG system.
Step 4 covers the data pipeline.
Monitor retrieval, generation and data freshness separately.
Map each metric to a failure.
This solution is correct. The plan covers the main failure points. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Monitoring each stage separately makes RAG failures diagnosable, not just detectable.
